name: Aaron Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI companies, unions and government. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, and I have a bachelor’s degree in accounting, but I am still a junior learning the tax codes. I match invoices to bank entries at an accounting firm, write the first return draft and take a marked-up file from the senior reviewer. I have never used an AI tool; my written checklist shows me where I went wrong. I enjoy seeing a bank entry finally match its invoice, but correcting the same tax code twice wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens when the office day ends?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I collect our two children from school while Miriam, my partner, repairs wooden furniture in her small shop. Our mortgage is covered, my junior pay is higher than usual, and we have about nine months of expenses saved. There are many accounting firms nearby, but I prefer learning steadily and earning my way before changing trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a short computer check is fine if a real accountant still signs the return. People bring us their books because they expect us to answer when a figure is questioned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage is covered by my wage and Miriam’s repair work, and we have nine months of expenses set aside. A little automation does not worry me, though I am still learning why some tax codes differ.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep matching client invoices to bank entries with my written checklist. In the first year I would ask my senior reviewer to demonstrate any required new check on a closed file during paid hours; I would not try an AI tool myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my pay and home. I dislike being told a new button is obvious when I am still learning the old steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is on the checklist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I write down which receipt I saw and which tax code I used, then my reviewer circles the ones I need to correct. The paper helps me remember what went wrong last time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm requires an AI check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI tools, but I would learn the firm’s approved check after a written rule and paid old-file demonstration. I would not put live client records into something I had not seen tested.

say: I would keep **human sign-off** on every client return.
I would ask for a **clear explanation** of any new routine check.
think: Our **nine-month cushion** and two wages make this picture secure.
I still need practice with **tax codes**, regardless of software.
do: Keep matching **invoices and bank entries** with my written checklist.
Learn a **required approved check** only after written rule and paid old-file demonstration.
feel: I feel **calm** about the household and cautious about unexplained buttons.
S0.quote: People bring us their books because they expect us to answer when a figure is questioned.
fieldNote: His **written checklist** is a learning aid, showing exactly which tax codes the senior reviewer corrected.
He has **nine months saved** and will accept only a firm-required tool after written instructions and paid demonstration.

steps.text: Keep matching client invoices to bank entries with written checklist
Learn approved AI check only after written job rule and paid demonstration

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the partners that a junior still needs real files to learn the trade. If software takes the easy returns, somebody has to explain how new staff will gain judgment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing notes and checking simple accounts take much of my week, so those hours could be cut. We have a strong reserve and plenty of firms nearby, but I would rather keep steady work than chase a title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask for a written shift forecast and keep working the client files assigned to me. If the approved AI checker becomes a written job requirement, I would take the paid demonstration; if my hours are cut in the first year, I would apply to advertised junior-accountant posts nearby only with written pay and hours no lower than now, staying until an offer and start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious that my paid hours could shrink, but the mortgage is secure for now. I would not tell the children a possible shift cut is a household emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain for a trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Miriam, my partner, repairs wooden furniture and has shown me how to sand a damaged chair. I would help after work, but I would not call myself a trained craftsperson on that basis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask a nearby firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether a senior accountant still reviews junior returns and whether the salary is written down. I am still learning and cannot replace supervision with a higher-sounding job title.

say: I would ask how **junior staff** learn when easy returns move to software.
I would request a **written shift forecast** before rumours spread.
think: My **simple account hours** could shrink under steady disruption.
A **strong reserve** and many local firms make a cut manageable.
do: Keep **assigned client files** and ask for a written shift forecast.
Take a **paid AI demonstration** only after written job requirement.
After a real cut, apply to **advertised junior posts** with written equal pay and hours while retaining shifts until start date.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible lost hours while our mortgage stays covered.
S1.quote: I am still learning and cannot replace supervision with a higher-sounding job title.
fieldNote: He prizes **apprenticeship-style supervision** and admits that helping with a chair does not make him a trained furniture worker.
The **local job search** starts after an actual cut, with written equal pay and current income protected until a start date.

steps.text: Keep assigned client files while seeking written shift forecast
Take paid approved-AI demonstration only after written job rule
Apply to advertised junior posts after cuts with written equal pay/hours; retain shifts until start date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2028 reaches the tax desk in 2028; capable robots for hands-on work arrive around 2031. I would want a written account of which junior shifts the firm expects to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my account-entry and draft-return shifts to go when AGI can do thinking work cheaply. Nine months of savings buys a search, but the unusually good junior wage may be hard to replace even with many nearby firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask for written notice of cuts and stop booking the family’s paid summer camp before the deposit is due. If my shifts fall in the first year after 2028, I would apply for advertised local accounting posts with written pay and hours at least equal to mine; if none offers that, I would arrange paid Saturday sanding at Miriam’s furniture shop only after we agree a rate and who watches our children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about replacing a good wage, but we have time to choose. The repair shop is hands-on until the later robots arrive, and I would still have to learn the craft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the shop have paid work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Miriam has a backlog of simple sanding jobs, but she would tell me which ones I can safely do and pay only for completed pieces. I would not take customer repairs home without her checking them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If capable robots reach furniture work around 2031, the Saturday work may fade too. I would treat furniture work as a bridge, not a promise that hands-on work stays safe.

say: I would say **AGI by 2028** reaches our tax desks before capable robots.
I would ask for **written junior-shift notice**.
think: I expect most **draft-return shifts** to disappear after 2028.
Our **nine-month reserve** buys time, but good junior pay may be hard to replace.
do: Stop booking **paid summer camp** before its deposit is due.
After lost shifts, seek **advertised local accounting work** with written equal pay and hours.
If no **equal-paid accounting offer** arrives, arrange Saturday sanding only with Miriam’s rate, supervision and childcare agreed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about income loss, with a usable reserve.
S2.quote: I would treat furniture work as a bridge, not a promise that hands-on work stays safe.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **2028 desk loss** from the possible 2031 effect on paid hands-on sanding work.
The **family shop bridge** is paid per completed piece, supervised by Miriam and conditional on childcare, rather than an assumed new career.

steps.text: Cancel paid summer camp booking before deposit is due
Seek advertised local accounting post after cuts with written equal pay and hours
Arrange paid Saturday sanding only if no equal-paid accounting offer, with rate, supervision and childcare agreed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell staff that AGI by 2031 gives us time to see what happens to tax work and learn a real trade if we choose. Capable robots arrive around 2034, so a hands-on move has its own deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years could let me build more money and learn furniture repair properly, but I still expect junior return preparation to shrink in 2031. I would not gamble our mortgage reserve on a romantic picture of a workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the accounting wage and ask Miriam whether I can apprentice in her furniture shop one paid Saturday a month, with childcare agreed. I would add 180 a month to cash savings while both wages hold; in the first year after 2031, if my tax shifts fall, I would take a vacant paid junior-accounting post with written equal pay and hours, or increase supervised shop days only if customer orders and our childcare schedule support it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years lets me learn how much sanding and repair I can actually do. I do not need to pretend a chair is a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does apprentice mean in that shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Miriam would show me joints and finishes, then inspect each piece before it goes to a customer. I would be paid for the Saturday hours rather than asked to work for free because we are family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if customer orders stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If customer orders stop, I would keep any paid account reviews and apply to advertised local firms before taking another shop day. I would not count work that is not booked.

say: I would point out the **2031 tax deadline** and later 2034 robot risk.
I would say a **real apprenticeship** needs paid supervised hours.
think: Our **mortgage reserve** must stay intact while I test furniture work.
do: Keep **accounting pay** and learn repair on paid supervised Saturdays with childcare agreed.
Save **180 monthly** while both household wages hold.
After lost shifts, seek **written equal-paid accounting work**; add shop days only with orders, otherwise keep paid reviews and search posted firms.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with time to test the shop before depending on it.
S3.quote: I do not need to pretend a chair is a pension.
fieldNote: The **paid apprenticeship** fits his traditional preference for learning by doing, with Miriam checking every customer piece.
His **income branches** require a real accounting vacancy or booked shop orders and childcare; he keeps current accounting pay while testing.

steps.text: Learn furniture repair on paid supervised Saturdays with childcare agreed
Save 180 monthly while both household wages hold
Take vacant paid accounting role with written equal pay/hours after cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to reduce mortgage debt and learn what people will still buy from a furniture maker. Robots around 2039 could reach the workshop after the tax desk changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years could see our children through school and give me time to become useful in the shop, but my tax-entry work still faces AGI in 2036. I would want the savings kept separate from workshop bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep preparing returns and take one paid supervised repair shift a month if Miriam agrees and we have childcare. I would first hold twelve months of household expenses in cash, then pay 200 monthly against the mortgage while both wages hold; in the first year after 2036, if my tax shifts fall, I would take a vacant accounting post with written pay and hours no lower than now, or work more shop shifts only while paid orders last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next few years, with work and savings. The long view makes me careful about the workshop’s own 2039 risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy new equipment for the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after customers pay for enough work to cover the equipment and leave the family reserve untouched. I would not borrow against our house for a sanding machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about careers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children to learn the work from someone patient and keep enough cash to choose. A family business can teach you, but it cannot guarantee your wage.

I would note **2039 robots** could reach the shop after tax desks change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my account-entry shifts could go before I have learned another paid skill. Written cut notice, a real local vacancy and paid supervised shop work would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who checks the chair after I sand it. Being family does not make me a craftsperson, and it should not make my hours free.

headlineQuote: Being family does not make me a craftsperson, and it should not make my hours free.
portrait: At **43**, Aaron is a junior accountant with a bachelor’s degree, still learning tax codes from marked-up files.
He and **partner Miriam** have two school-age children, a mortgage, high junior pay and nine months saved.
He has **never used AI**, values supervised paid learning and can consider many nearby accounting firms.
The **2028 scenario** threatens his account-entry hours; longer runways let him test paid furniture repair while guarding family savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his junior account-entry shifts before he has another paid skill.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice**, a real local vacancy and paid supervised shop work with childcare.
